title: Serving Voice AI at $1/hr: Open-source, LoRAs, Latency, Load Balancing - Neil Dwyer, Gabber
talk_summary: Neil Dwyer describes hosting the open-source Orpheus voice model on L40S GPUs for real-time AI personas, covering LoRA fine-tunes for voice cloning, latency budgeting, and load balancing. The core lessons are about GPU inference serving (batching, FP8 quantization, consistent-hash routing), not agent orchestration.

takeaways.technique: Consistent-hash sticky routing to warm caches
takeaways.what_they_do: They hash session IDs onto a consistent hash ring of GPU servers so a whole session stays on the GPU that already has the needed LoRA loaded, avoiding reloads and rebalancing storms when servers are removed.
They switched the model to FP8 dynamic quantization, which needs no calibration data, to get above real-time throughput on cheaper L40S GPUs instead of H100s.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they support FP8 dynamic quantization which requires basically zero work... It just works automatically
takeaways.numbers: FP16 was slower than real time on L40S; FP8 reached 105 tok/s (95 tok/s with LoRA, batch 10)

takeaways.technique: Batch concurrent generations on one GPU
takeaways.what_they_do: They require batch inference so multiple generations (and multiple LoRAs) share one GPU concurrently, which is what makes the $1/hr economics work.
They found the base model emitted ~600ms of leading silence, wasting compute; instead of only filtering it at playback, they fine-tuned the silence away in their LoRA clones.
They define a latency budget and start downstream work (LLM generation) during the endpointing 'snooze' window so the first audio packet lands inside budget.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if we generate the first audio packet within that snooze period, then we're kind of like in the money on on latency
takeaways.numbers: 1.5s is the acceptable threshold; 0.5-1s is the sweet spot
